title: The 10 Best Corded Impact Wrenches
subtitle: Wired impact wrenches ranked from live Amazon data — the corded impact tool for lug nuts and bolts.
intro: Quick note on names: there is no such thing as a corded impact driver — the impact-driver format (1/4-inch hex, for screws) is inherently cordless. The corded impact tool that actually exists is the impact wrench: a 1/2-inch square drive that spins sockets to break loose and tighten lug nuts, suspension bolts, and rusted hardware. This list covers electric corded impact wrenches — the ones that plug into a wall outlet (120V) or a car's 12V socket. If you want to drive screws, you want an impact driver from the cordless list; if you want to wrench on a car without an air compressor, you're in the right place.

products.name: Eastvolt 800W 7.5-Amp Corded Impact Wrench
products.verdict: The value pick: a genuine 7.5-amp corded impact wrench for about $43, rated for 450 ft-lbs, with 1,200 reviews behind it. It plugs into the wall and breaks loose lug nuts for a third of the CRAFTSMAN's price.
pros: Comes with four lug-nut sockets and a carry case
cons: 4.2 stars, a step below the CRAFTSMAN
Off-brand support

products.name: CRAFTSMAN CMEF901 7.5-Amp 1/2" Corded Impact Wrench (450 ft-lbs)
products.verdict: The best corded impact wrench you can buy new right now. 450 ft-lbs from a wall outlet, a hog-ring anvil, a variable-speed trigger, and 712 reviews at 4.5 stars. It costs more than the off-brand 7.5-amp wrenches, and the brand and track record are what you're paying for.
pros: 450 ft-lbs of breakaway torque from a wall outlet
cons: About three times the price of the Eastvolt
8.7 lb, heavy for overhead work

products.name: Wagan EL2257 12V DC 1/2" Impact Wrench (automotive)
products.verdict: A roadside impact wrench that runs off your car's 12V socket — perfect for the trunk when you get a flat far from an outlet. Not shop-grade power, but 1,300 reviews say it does the tire-change job.
pros: Runs off a 12V car socket — works roadside
cons: 12V has far less power than an AC or air wrench
Won't budge badly rusted or overtightened nuts

products.name: 12-Volt 1/2" Car Impact Wrench (400 N·m claimed)
products.verdict: Another 12V roadside wrench, with a bold 400 N·m / 300 ft-lb claim. Treat that number with skepticism — a 12V socket can't feed that in the real world — but as a spare-tire tool it's fine.
cons: Torque claim is optimistic for 12V
Light-duty only

products.name: WEN 7.5-Amp Two-Direction Corded Impact Wrench
products.verdict: WEN's value formula applied to an AC impact wrench — a real 7.5-amp motor with a hog-ring anvil for around $50. A sensible budget alternative to the Eastvolt from a known value brand.
cons: Small review base so far
Basic build

products.name: K Tool 81380A 1/2" Electric Impact Wrench
products.verdict: From K Tool International, a real automotive tool brand. A straightforward corded 1/2-inch impact wrench at the low end of the price range — newer to Amazon, but a legitimate name in the trade.
pros: Low price for an AC impact wrench
cons: Very few reviews on Amazon yet
Basic feature set

products.name: DEKOPRO 4-Amp Corded Impact Wrench (3,600 rpm)
products.verdict: A compact, lighter-duty corded impact wrench from budget brand DEKOPRO. The 4-amp motor is modest, but for light automotive and household bolts at a low price it fills a gap.
pros: Compact and light for a corded wrench
cons: 4 amps is light-duty for stuck bolts
Very few reviews yet

products.name: OEMTOOLS 24666 1/2" Drive Heavy Duty Corded Impact Wrench (8.5 Amp, 400 ft-lbs)
products.verdict: The strongest motor on the list: 8.5 amps, 400 ft-lbs of breakaway torque, and a cast-aluminum gear housing, for well under the CRAFTSMAN's price. A solid garage wrench if you want more motor than the budget picks.
pros: 8.5-amp motor, the most on this list
Cast-aluminum gear housing, hog-ring anvil, rocker forward/reverse
cons: 8.8 lb, the heaviest here
Sold by a third-party seller, not Amazon

products.name: Hammerhead HDIW075 7.5-Amp 1/2" Corded Impact Wrench
products.verdict: A well-reviewed 7.5-amp wrench with a metal gearbox and a friction-ring anvil, 686 reviews at 4.5 stars. Its 240 ft-lbs rating is lower than the 400-450 ft-lb wrenches here, so it suits normal lug nuts better than seized suspension bolts.
cons: 240 ft-lbs, well below the 450 ft-lb picks
Current listing is a third-party seller with low stock and paid shipping

products.name: Hyperion Lift-Assist 12V Portable Impact Wrench by Deltran (043-1003-HY-WH)
products.verdict: A roadside 12V wrench that runs off the cigarette lighter or clips straight to the car battery. It comes in a hard case with a work light, two lug-nut sockets and a spare fuse, so it can live in the trunk for flat-tire days.
pros: Cigarette-lighter cable and battery clamps both included
Hard case, LED work light, two reversible lug-nut sockets
3.1 lb, easy to keep in the trunk
cons: 12V power is light-duty next to an AC wrench
Small review base so far

avoid.name: Ingersoll Rand 231C 1/2" Air Impact Wrench
avoid.flag: Excellent tool — but it's pneumatic and needs an air compressor
avoid.verdict: To be clear, this is a superb impact wrench and a shop standard. The catch: it's pneumatic. It doesn't plug into a wall outlet; it needs a good-sized air compressor to run. Buy it only if you already have one.
reasons: It runs on compressed air, not electricity. There's no plug — you need an air compressor (realistically a $200+ pancake or larger) and a hose to use it at all.
A small hobby compressor can't keep up with it; it wants real CFM, so the true cost is the wrench plus a capable compressor.
If you want to plug into a wall outlet and go, buy the CRAFTSMAN or Eastvolt above instead. They're corded-electric, no air needed.
It's on this 'avoid' list only because it's the wrong category for someone shopping electric impact wrenches — in a shop with air, it's a great buy.

buyers_guide.a: An impact driver has a 1/4-inch hex chuck for driving screws and small fasteners — and it's a cordless-only format. An impact wrench has a 1/2-inch (or 3/8") square drive that spins sockets to loosen and tighten bolts and lug nuts. If you want to drive screws, see the cordless impact drivers.

AC corded wrenches plug into a wall outlet for shop-grade power. 12V wrenches run off a car socket for roadside tire changes — handy but light-duty. Air (pneumatic) wrenches are powerful but need an air compressor. This list focuses on the electric ones you can plug in.

A corded electric impact wrench gives sustained power for less money than a comparable cordless model, and never runs out of charge — good for a home garage with an outlet. Cordless wins only if you need to work far from power.

buyers_guide.q: How much torque do I need?
buyers_guide.a: For car lug nuts (usually 80-100 ft-lbs to spec, more when rusted or over-torqued), aim for a wrench rated around 300-450 ft-lbs of breakaway so it actually cracks them loose. The 12V roadside tools sit well below that — fine for a spare, not for stuck bolts.

It's a socket retainer that lets you push sockets on and pull them off by hand — fast and convenient. A detent-pin anvil holds sockets more securely but is slower to change. For general use, a hog ring is the friendlier choice.
